lec05kp21-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp21-u01-p1-title.text: The SVM solution resembles a Parzen expansion but uses 19 kernels, not 120

lec05kp21-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p1-bridge.text: In KP20 only 22 points of the kernel perceptron had $\alpha>0$. The SVM solution is also a sum of kernels, so how many kernels does it use?

lec05kp21-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-sparse
lec05kp21-u01-p1-fig1.text: The 120 ring training points: on the left the 120 Parzen kernels, on the right the SVM keeping only 19 (grey dots have coefficient 0).

image.alt: The 120 ring training points: on the left the 120 Parzen kernels, on the right the SVM keeping only 19 (grey dots have coefficient 0).

lec05kp21-u01-p1-term:稀疏解.name: term:Sparse solution
lec05kp21-u01-p1-term:稀疏解.text: **Sparse solution**: an expansion in which most coefficients are 0 and only a few terms are really used.

lec05kp21-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p1-c1.text: **The SVM solution**: $g(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}a_iK(x,x_i)+w_0$, $a_i=\lambda_iy_i$; like a Parzen expansion with a Gaussian kernel.

lec05kp21-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p1-c2.text: **Two differences**: (1) $g$ is not a density; (2) Parzen uses all $N$ points, the SVM only the $N_s$ support vectors. Rings (KP19 data, $C=10$, $\gamma=0.5$): 19 of 120, 96.8% on new points.

lec05kp21-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp21-u01-p2-title.text: The representer theorem: searched in an infinite-dimensional space, the answer is just N kernels

lec05kp21-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p2-bridge.text: The SVM solution sums kernels over the support vectors only. Why is the answer a finite sum of kernels when we search a possibly infinite-dimensional space?

lec05kp21-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-rep
lec05kp21-u01-p2-fig1.text: The representer theorem: the minimizer of the data term plus Ω(‖g‖) is g(x)=Σⱼ aⱼ K(x,xⱼ) with only N coefficients.

image.alt: The representer theorem: the minimizer of the data term plus Ω(‖g‖) is g(x)=Σⱼ aⱼ K(x,xⱼ) with only N coefficients.

lec05kp21-u01-p2-term:Representer 定理.name: term:Representer theorem
lec05kp21-u01-p2-term:Representer 定理.text: **Representer theorem**: the minimizer in the RKHS of the regularized cost $\sum_i\mathcal L(g(x_i),y_i)+\Omega(\|g\|)$ has a minimizer of the form $g(x)=\sum_{j=1}^Na_jK(x,x_j)$.

lec05kp21-u01-p2-term:正則化項.name: term:Regularization term
lec05kp21-u01-p2-term:正則化項.text: **Regularization term** $\Omega(\|g\|)$: a penalty on the norm of the solution (strictly increasing) that keeps it small and simple.

lec05kp21-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p2-c1.text: **Why it is striking**: the search space may be infinite-dimensional, yet the best solution is a combination of $N$ kernels placed on the training points, leaving $N$ coefficients. $\mathcal L$ may be any non-negative loss.

lec05kp21-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp21-u01-p3-title.text: A numerical check: the 6-D w equals the N-kernel combination, within 2×10⁻¹⁴

lec05kp21-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p3-bridge.text: The representer theorem makes the minimizer a sum of $N$ kernels. Can we check it in a small space?

lec05kp21-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-repcheck
lec05kp21-u01-p3-fig1.text: The 6-D check with the quadratic kernel: w and Φᵀa differ by at most 1.9e-14 and predictions by at most 2.2e-14.

image.alt: The 6-D check with the quadratic kernel: w and Φᵀa differ by at most 1.9e-14 and predictions by at most 2.2e-14.

lec05kp21-u01-p3-term:Gram 矩陣.name: term:Gram matrix
lec05kp21-u01-p3-term:Gram 矩陣.text: **Gram matrix** $\mathcal K$: the $N\times N$ array of $K(x_i,x_j)$.

lec05kp21-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p3-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): quadratic kernel, 6 features; 30 random points and targets, $C=0.7$. 6-D: $w=(\Phi^T\Phi+CI)^{-1}\Phi^Ty$; kernel: $a=(\mathcal K+CI)^{-1}y$.

lec05kp21-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p3-c2.text: **Result**: $w$ and $\Phi^Ta$ differ by at most $1.9\times10^{-14}$; predictions on new points by at most $2.2\times10^{-14}$.

lec05kp21-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p3-c3.text: **Meaning**: $w=\sum_ja_j\phi(x_j)$ lies in the span of the training features, a special case of the theorem.

lec05kp21-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp21-u01-p4-title.text: Kernel least squares: put the form in and a = 𝒦⁻¹y, a single linear system

lec05kp21-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p4-bridge.text: $w$ lies in the span of the training points. Put this form into the squared error: how is $a$ solved?

lec05kp21-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-hand
lec05kp21-u01-p4-fig1.text: Kernel least squares on two training points: g=1−2x passes through both targets at C=0, while g=0.2−0.6x is pulled toward 0 at C=1.

image.alt: Kernel least squares on two training points: g=1−2x passes through both targets at C=0, while g=0.2−0.6x is pulled toward 0 at C=1.

lec05kp21-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p4-c1.text: **Substituting**: $J(a)=(y-\mathcal Ka)^T(y-\mathcal Ka)$; a zero gradient gives $a=\mathcal K^{-1}y$ and $g(x)=y^T\mathcal K^{-1}p$ with $p=[K(x,x_1),\dots,K(x,x_N)]^T$ ($\mathcal K$ must be invertible).

lec05kp21-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p4-c2.text: **By hand** (designed here): points $x=0,1$, targets $+1,-1$, kernel $K=xz+1$: $\mathcal K=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $a=(3,-2)$, $g(x)=3-2(x+1)=1-2x$, $g(0.5)=0$.

lec05kp21-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p4-c3.text: **Note**: this solution is not sparse; all the $a_j$ are usually nonzero.

lec05kp21-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp21-u01-p5-title.text: Nine noisy points: an exact fit, 9 nonzero coefficients, error 0.047 against sin

lec05kp21-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p5-bridge.text: The solution is not sparse and the $a_j$ are usually nonzero. With noisy data does kernel least squares pass through every point, and how far is it from the true curve?

lec05kp21-u01-p5-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-sin
lec05kp21-u01-p5-fig1.text: Nine noisy points and sin x: C=0 passes through every point, C=0.1 is closest to sin and C=10 is flattened.

image.alt: Nine noisy points and sin x: C=0 passes through every point, C=0.1 is closest to sin and C=10 is flattened.

lec05kp21-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p5-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): $y=\sin x+$ noise (sd 0.2), 9 points, Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\|x-z\|^2/2\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma=0.8$; the condition number of $\mathcal K$ is 49.

lec05kp21-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p5-c2.text: **Result**: all 9 $a_j$ are nonzero (largest 2.82); the training error is 0, passing through every point; the mean squared error against the true $\sin x$ is 0.047.

lec05kp21-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p5-c3.text: **Honestly**: with these settings the curve does not oscillate wildly; passing through the noise points is the direction of overfitting, but the size is modest.

lec05kp21-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp21-u01-p6-title.text: With 𝒦+C·I: C=0.1 gives error 0.033 against sin, and C≥10 flattens the curve

lec05kp21-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p6-bridge.text: Passing through every noisy point gave an error of 0.047. Replacing $\mathcal K$ by $\mathcal K+CI$, which $C$ is good?

lec05kp21-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-csweep
lec05kp21-u01-p6-fig1.text: Training error and error against sin versus C: the smallest error against sin is 0.033 at C=0.1 and C≥10 flattens the curve.

image.alt: Training error and error against sin versus C: the smallest error against sin is 0.033 at C=0.1 and C≥10 flattens the curve.

lec05kp21-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p6-c1.text: **The fix**: $a=(\mathcal K+CI)^{-1}y$; $C=0$ is kernel least squares and a larger $C$ squeezes the norm of the solution; $CI$ also makes the matrix easier to invert.

lec05kp21-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p6-c3.text: **Meaning**: a small $C$ passes through the noise and a large one flattens the curve; all 9 $a_j$ stay nonzero for every $C$, so $CI$ creates no sparsity.

lec05kp21-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp21-u01-p7-title.text: Sparsity needs ½‖w‖² and a fitting C and γ: otherwise nearly all points are support vectors

lec05kp21-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p7-bridge.text: Adding $CI$ creates no sparsity, as all 9 coefficients stay nonzero for every $C$. Why does the SVM have so few support vectors?

lec05kp21-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-svcount
lec05kp21-u01-p7-fig1.text: Support vectors against C on the rings for γ=0.01, 0.5 and 50: 19 at γ=0.5, C=10 and about 116 at γ=50.

image.alt: Support vectors against C on the rings for γ=0.01, 0.5 and 50: 19 at γ=0.5, C=10 and about 116 at γ=50.

lec05kp21-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p7-c1.text: **The source**: in $J=\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum I(\xi_i)$ the term $\|w\|^2$ is a regularization term that implicitly drives most $\lambda_i$ to 0.

lec05kp21-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p7-c2.text: **Experiment** (designed here, 120 ring points, $\gamma=0.5$) support vectors (new points): $C=0.01$: 120 (94.3%); $C=1$: 39 (97.3%); $C=10$: 19 (96.8%); $C=1000$: 13 (95.4%).

lec05kp21-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p7-c3.text: **Not automatic** (this $C$ is the SVM penalty, the opposite of the ridge $C$): $\gamma=50$: 116 whatever $C$ (86.8%); $\gamma=0.01$, $C=1$: 120 (71.5%).

lec05kp21-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp21-u01-p8-title.text: Other routes to sparsity: a dictionary keeps 17 of the 120 points (threshold 0.7)

lec05kp21-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p8-bridge.text: The sparsity of the SVM comes from the regularization term, but when $\gamma$ is too large nearly every point is a support vector. Is there another way to cut the number of kernels?

lec05kp21-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-dict
lec05kp21-u01-p8-fig1.text: The dictionary method on 120 ring points: 17 kept at threshold 0.7 (circles); thresholds 0.99, 0.9, 0.7 and 0.5 keep 90, 38, 17 and 9.

image.alt: The dictionary method on 120 ring points: 17 kept at threshold 0.7 (circles); thresholds 0.99, 0.9, 0.7 and 0.5 keep 90, 38, 17 and 9.

lec05kp21-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp21-u01-p8-c1.text: **Four routes** (source): RVM (Bayesian prior, sparser, cubic cost); online kernel LMS (norm constraint); projection (hyperball, linear cost); dictionary (keep a point only if its similarity is below a threshold, quadratic cost).

lec05kp21-u01-p8-c2.name: u01-p8-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p8-c2.text: **Dictionary experiment** (designed here, 120 ring points, $\gamma=0.5$): threshold 0.99 keeps 90; 0.9: 38; 0.7: 17; 0.5: 9.

lec05kp21-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p8-c3.text: **To remember**: the representer theorem leaves $N$ coefficients; the SVM zeroes most by regularization, a dictionary by a threshold.

lec05kp21-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp21-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: too many support vectors hurt: 116 of them give only 86.8% at γ=50

lec05kp21-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p9-bridge.text: A dictionary keeps 17 of the 120 points at threshold 0.7. Are fewer support vectors always better and more always worse?

lec05kp21-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-dense
lec05kp21-u01-p9-fig1.text: Table of support-vector counts and new-point accuracy: 19 with 96.9%, 13 with 95.4%, 120 with 94.3%, 39 with 97.3% and 116 with 86.8%.

image.alt: Table of support-vector counts and new-point accuracy: 19 with 96.9%, 13 with 95.4%, 120 with 94.3%, 39 with 97.3% and 116 with 86.8%.

lec05kp21-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp21-u01-p9-c2.text: **The source's reminder**: when there are too many support vectors, generalization degrades.

lec05kp21-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp21-u01-p9-c3.text: **But few does not guarantee good** (one run, the gap may be noise): at $\gamma=0.5$, $C=1$, 39 support vectors give 97.3%, better than 13 with 95.4%; the count is a clue, not a goal.

lec05kp21-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp21-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, kernel least squares on two points with C=1

lec05kp21-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p10-bridge.text: The count of support vectors is only a clue. Back to the smallest example, the two-point hand calculation: with $C=1$, how do $a$ and $g$ change?

lec05kp21-u01-p10-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-practice
lec05kp21-u01-p10-fig1.text: Practice figure: training points x=0 and 1, targets +1 and −1, kernel xz+1; question 1 finds a and g for C=1 and question 2 compares with C=0.

image.alt: Practice figure: training points x=0 and 1, targets +1 and −1, kernel xz+1; question 1 finds a and g for C=1 and question 2 compares with C=0.

lec05kp21-u01-p10-q2.name: u01-p10-q2
lec05kp21-u01-p10-q2.text: **Question 1**: for $C=1$ solve $a=(\mathcal K+I)^{-1}y$ and find $g(0)$ and $g(1)$.

lec05kp21-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp21-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: compared with $g(0)=1$, $g(1)=-1$ at $C=0$, what did $C$ do to the solution?

lec05kp21-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp21-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2, with C=1 pulling g toward 0

lec05kp21-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp21-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked to find $g(0)$ and $g(1)$ for kernel least squares on two points with $C=1$ and to compare with $C=0$. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp21-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp21-practice-sol
lec05kp21-u01-p11-fig1.text: a=(0.8,−0.6), g(0)=0.2 and g(1)=−0.4; they are 1 and −1 at C=0, so C=1 pulls the solution toward 0.

image.alt: a=(0.8,−0.6), g(0)=0.2 and g(1)=−0.4; they are 1 and −1 at C=0, so C=1 pulls the solution toward 0.

lec05kp21-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp21-u01-p11-a3.text: **Question 2**: at $C=0$ they are $+1$ and $-1$ (an exact fit) and $C=1$ shrinks them to $0.2$ and $-0.4$: $C$ pulls the solution toward 0, and both coefficients stay nonzero.

steps.label: Representer and sparsity
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. The difference between the SVM solution and the Parzen expansion, the representer theorem, the closed form of kernel least squares, sparsity coming from the regularization term, the four routes to sparsification and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number (19 of 120 support vectors, the 6-D check with a gap of 1.9e-14, the hand result a=(3,-2), the errors 0.047 and 0.033 on 9 noisy points, the support-vector table, the dictionary 17 of 120, the practice a=(0.8,-0.6)) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added); the pages state honestly that kernel least squares did not oscillate wildly with these settings, that adding CI does not create sparsity and that nearly every point is a support vector when gamma is too large or C too small. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: A sparse solution
steps.speakerNotes: In KP20 only 22 points of the kernel perceptron had alpha above 0. This page asks how many kernels the SVM solution uses, since it is also a sum of kernels. First a sparse solution: an expansion in which most coefficients are 0 and only a few terms are really used. The SVM solution is the sum over the support vectors of a_i times K, plus w0, with a_i equal to lambda_i times y_i; with a Gaussian kernel it resembles a Parzen expansion. Two differences: first, g is not a density and does not integrate to 1; second, the number of terms: Parzen uses all N points, the SVM only the support vectors. Rings with the KP19 data, C equal to 10 and gamma equal to 0.5: only 19 of the 120 training points are support vectors, with 96.8% on new points. The left of the figure is the 120 Parzen kernels and the right the 19 of the SVM. The next page asks why the best solution is always a finite sum of kernels.

steps.label: The representer theorem
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the SVM uses only 19 kernels. This page asks why the answer is a finite sum of kernels when we search a possibly infinite-dimensional space. First the representer theorem: the minimizer in the RKHS of the regularized cost, a data term L plus Omega of the norm, must be a sum of N kernels, one on each training point. Then the regularization term: a penalty on the norm of the solution, Omega strictly increasing, that keeps it small and simple. Why it is striking: the search space may be infinite-dimensional, yet the best solution has only N coefficients, and L may be any non-negative loss. The next page checks it with numbers.

steps.label: A numerical check
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the theorem makes the minimizer a sum of N kernels. This page asks whether it can be checked in a small space we can see. First the Gram matrix: the N by N array of K of x_i and x_j. The setup was designed here: the quadratic kernel has 6 explicit features; 30 random points and targets, C equal to 0.7. Solve w directly in 6-D, then solve a with the kernel. The result: w and Phi transpose times a differ by at most 1.9 times 10 to the minus 14, and predictions on new points by at most 2.2 times 10 to the minus 14. The meaning is that w is the sum of a_j times phi of x_j and lies in the span of the training feature vectors, a special case of the theorem with squared loss plus the squared norm of w. The next page asks how a is solved when this form is put into the squared error.

steps.label: Kernel least squares
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said w lies in the span of the training points. This page asks how a is solved when this form is put into the squared error. Substituting: J is the squared norm of y minus K a, a zero gradient gives a equal to the inverse of K times y, and g of x is y transpose times the inverse of K times p, with p the vector of K of x with x_1 up to x_N; K must be invertible. The hand example was designed here: points x equal to 0 and 1, targets +1 and -1, kernel K equal to xz plus 1: the Gram matrix is [[1, 1], [1, 2]], a is (3, -2), g of x is 3 minus 2 times x plus 1, which is 1 minus 2x, and g of 0.5 is 0. Note: this solution is not sparse and all the a_j are usually nonzero. The next page asks what happens when the data are noisy.

steps.label: Noisy data
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the solution is not sparse and the a_j are usually nonzero. This page asks whether kernel least squares passes through every point on noisy data and how far it is from the true curve. The setup was designed here: y equal to sin x plus noise with standard deviation 0.2, 9 points and a Gaussian kernel with sigma 0.8; the condition number of the Gram matrix is 49. The result: all 9 a_j are nonzero, the largest being 2.82; the training error is 0, passing through every point; the mean squared error against the true sin x is 0.047. Honestly: with these settings the curve does not oscillate wildly; passing through the noise points is the direction of overfitting, but the size is modest. The next page asks which C to use when K is replaced by K plus C I.

steps.label: Adding C·I
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said passing through every noisy point gave an error of 0.047. This page asks which C is good when K is replaced by K plus C I. The fix: a is the inverse of K plus C I times y; C equal to 0 is kernel least squares and a larger C squeezes the norm of the solution; C I also makes the matrix easier to invert. Results, training error and error against sin: C of 0.01 gives 0.0003 and 0.043; C of 0.1 gives 0.0063 and 0.033, the best; C of 1 gives 0.078 and 0.079; C of 10 gives 0.349 and 0.355; C of 100 gives 0.465 and 0.479. The meaning is that a small C passes through the noise and a large one flattens the curve; all 9 a_j stay nonzero for every C, so C I creates no sparsity. The next page asks where the sparsity of the SVM comes from.

steps.label: Where sparsity comes from
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said adding C I gave no sparsity and every a_j stayed nonzero. This page asks why the SVM has so few support vectors. The source: in the cost J, one half of the squared norm of w plus C times the error term, the squared norm of w is a regularization term that implicitly drives most lambda to 0. The experiment was designed here: 120 ring points and gamma 0.5, support vectors and new-point accuracy: C of 0.01 gives 120 and 94.3%; C of 1 gives 39 and 97.3%; C of 10 gives 19 and 96.8%; C of 1000 gives 13 and 95.4%. But sparsity is not automatic: at gamma 50 there are 116 whatever C, with 86.8%; at gamma 0.01 and C of 1 there are 120, with 71.5%. The next page asks whether another way can reduce the number of kernels.

steps.label: Routes to sparsity
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the sparsity of the SVM comes from the regularization term but that nearly every point is a support vector when gamma is too large. This page asks whether another way can cut the number of kernels. Four routes, as the source says: RVM, a Bayesian prior, sparser but with memory growing with the square and computation with the cube of the basis count; online adaptation, kernel LMS with a norm constraint; projection, a hyperball constraint equal to a forgetting factor, linear cost; and the dictionary, adding a point only if its similarity is below a threshold, quadratic cost. The dictionary experiment was designed here: 120 ring points, gamma 0.5, points arriving one by one: threshold 0.99 keeps 90; 0.9 keeps 38; 0.7 keeps 17; 0.5 keeps 9. To remember: the representer theorem turns an infinite-dimensional search into N coefficients and the regularization term decides how many are zero. The next extension page looks at the number of support vectors and how good the result is.

steps.label: Extension: few is not always good
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said a dictionary can cut 120 kernels to 17. This extension asks whether fewer support vectors are always better and more always worse. The comparison was designed here, with C equal to 1000: gamma 0.01 gives 19 support vectors and 96.9%; gamma 0.5 gives 13 and 95.4%; gamma 50 gives 116 and 86.8%. The source's reminder: when there are too many support vectors, generalization degrades. But few does not guarantee good: at gamma 0.5 and C of 1, 39 support vectors give 97.3%, better than 13 with 95.4%; the count is a clue, not a goal. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the count of support vectors is only a clue. This page poses an exercise back on the two-point hand example: training points x equal to 0 and 1, targets +1 and -1, kernel K equal to xz plus 1; g of x is a_1 times K of x with 0 plus a_2 times K of x with 1. Question 1: for C equal to 1 solve a as the inverse of K plus I times y and find g of 0 and g of 1. Question 2: compared with g of 0 equal to 1 and g of 1 equal to -1 at C equal to 0, what did C do to the solution? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: K plus I is [[2, 1], [1, 3]] with determinant 5 and inverse one fifth of [[3, -1], [-1, 2]]; a is one fifth of (3 plus 1, minus 1 minus 2), which is (0.8, -0.6). Values: g of 0 is 0.8 times 1 minus 0.6 times 1, which is 0.2; g of 1 is 0.8 times 1 minus 0.6 times 2, which is -0.4. Question 2: at C equal to 0 they are +1 and -1, an exact fit; C equal to 1 shrinks them to 0.2 and -0.4, so C pulls the solution toward 0, and both coefficients stay nonzero. That finishes the representer theorem and sparsification; the next knowledge point looks at robust statistical regression and ridge regression.
